Design Miami , one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.
The theme, Unveiling , calls for the viewers to truly observe each object, deciphering what inspired the artist to create them, and the surrounding stories behind their choices. These may be hiding in plain sight or several times removed from the final result, reflecting something deeply personal or rooted in the artist’s culture. Unveiling is then divided among four curatorial threads, each with different approaches and best represented by certain artists, techniques, and galleries.
Pippin Drysdale, “Sacred Lands,” 2026. Adrian Sassoon at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Adrian Sassoon, London; photography by Robert Frith, Acorn Photo.)
First up is Process as Aesthetic: Unveiling the Hand of the Maker . This theme highlights the creative process, particularly the techniques, labor, and experimentation that come to determine an object’s aesthetic, regarding these steps as a vehicle for expression. This can be seen in the ceramic works of Bouke de Vries and Pippin Drysdale; Caroline Desile’s architecture-influenced Totem 1 ; Richard Haining’s STACKED creations, made up of thousands of pieces of salvaged New York City wood; and Man Ray’s Optic-Topic mask , the centerpiece of this division.
Le Corbusier, “La licorne passe sur la mer,” 1959. Boccara Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Boccara Gallery.)
Meanwhile, Subverting Archetypes: The Familiar, Reimagined , takes a more surrealist route, blurring the line between the familiar and the uncanny, asking viewers to reassess to what they think they know. Such is the case of a selection of 20th-century tapestries by Le Corbusier, Sonia Delaunay, and Alexander Calder. This section also features the work of Brazilian designer Lucas Recchia, who blends metal with fused glass, and a wall piece by Jaydan Moore, who turns found, silver-plated tableware into sculptural forms.
Dee Clements, “Gams,” 2026. Mindy Solomon Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: Clare Britt, courtesy of the artist and Mindy Solomon Gallery)

The remote village of Igiugig, Alaska, has given the world a masterclass in solidarity. Even more impressive, they did so despite only having a population of about 70 people. When a medical evacuation team couldn’t land at the local airport to help a child because the runway lights were broken, the city showed up, lining up their cars to guide the plane with their headlights.
It all started when Ida Nelson, head tribal clerk based in this small southwest Alaska village, heard a loud noise after 11:30 PM on August 28, 2020. “When they first flew over, I was like ‘oh my gosh,’ that sounds like a weird vehicle. I’ve never heard that truck before. And it wasn’t a truck, it was an airplane,” Nelson told KTOO . “Anytime there’s any type of planes flying after dark, you always assume it’s going to be something urgent and an emergency.”
And it was an emergency: a LifeMed Alaska crew was trying to land. When Nelson, who lives close to the airport, looked outside, she realized the runway lights weren't working. Worried, she got in her truck, where she met a local pilot who had also noticed the issue. While pilots can usually turn runway lights from their aircraft, that didn’t work this time. Nelson and the pilot also tried turning on the lights manually from the ground to no avail.
Concerned, Nelson offered to light up one end of the runway with her truck, but they still needed more help. And so, Nelson’s neighbor rallied the community, making 32 phone calls. Meanwhile, the pilot hopped into his own plane and contacted the LifeMed crew. “I was feeling nervous, anxious because this is late at night and this is someone’s child,” Nelson told CNN . “The only thing I could think of was how quickly I could get other people here to help because what if that was my baby’s plane?”
Within 20 minutes, 20 people had shown up in their vehicles, many in their pajamas, ready to follow the plane crew’s instructions. The townspeople staggered their cars and 4-wheelers along the runway so the pilot could see end to end. The people remained in place as the plane landed, boarded the patient, and departed safely for Anchorage, where the young patient made it to the hospital in stable condition.

items.text:
Another of the infamous gentleman art thief “Erik the Belgian’s” heists have been solved.
For nearly half a century, a 13th-century carving of the Virgin Mary sat in a Spanish police database as an unsolved case.
The Romanesque sculpture vanished in 1979 from the Church of San Pedro de Meoz, a small parish in Navarre, swept up in a wave of church robberies that hit rural Spain hard where rich heritage was paired with almost no security.
The man blamed for it was René Alphonse van den Berghe, better known as Erik the Belgian, one of the most prolific art thieves in Modern history.
Now, at last, the piece is back where it belongs. Spain’s National Police announced its recovery from a collection in the United Kingdom, closing a trail that ran through Belgium, London and the Netherlands.
The sculpture is a seated walnut-wood Virgin, still carrying traces of its original gilding and polychrome, measuring 54 centimeters tall and holding the figure of the Christ Child—though she’s missing both forearms. Small enough to wrap in a blanket, valuable enough to disappear into the antiques trade for decades, that combination made her exactly Erik’s type.
A veritable manifestation of the fictional Arsène Lupin, Van den Berghe (1940–2020) robbed churches and monasteries across sparsely populated parts of his adopted country of Spain and elsewhere in Europe.
Thousands of crimes have been attributed to him, much of it involving medieval sacred art. He was also a painter and a forger, and in his later years leaned hard on his reputation as a “gentleman thief,” giving interviews, recounting heists, and even helping recover some of his own marks.
In 2023, GNN reported that a two-foot by two-foot square cut away from the bottom left corner of a 17th-century tapestry was recovered with the help of none other than the man who had held the scissors: The Belgian.
Van den Berghe’s most famous job was the 1980 theft of the silver Ark of Sant Martirià from the monastery of Sant Esteve de Banyoles in Girona, the prized reliquary of the town’s patron saint forged from silver in the 15th century.
The investigation into the Virgin Mary work was restarted in April after authorities got a useful lead, and quickly confirmed a long-suspected method of Erik: the loot went out by road to countries with hungrier art and antiques markets.

items.text:
More than 400 years after the Pilgrims first explored the Cape Cod area, land belonging to Native Americans was returned to Indigenous ownership.
On October 30, The Nature Conservancy gave roughly 126 acres of salt marsh and natural habitat in Eastham, Massachusetts to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit based in Mashpee. The land sits right next to a 20.4-acre parcel the Conservancy bought earlier in the year for $3 million, linking them into a larger protected area that looks out over First Encounter Beach. ⁠
“This place holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed,” Ramona Peters, founder and board president of the Native Land Conservancy and a member of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, said in a published statement . “Long before the first encounter, Native people lived here and took care of this land.”
In December 1620, not long after the Mayflower arrived, an exploring party led by Myles Standish traded arrows and gunfire with Nauset warriors near what’s now called First Encounter Beach, named for the first hostile meeting between the Pilgrims and a native people.
The fight came after colonists had taken corn and disturbed graves. “Our ancestors weren’t just standing around. They were protecting their families, and taking care of this land lets us tell that story the right way,” R. Peters said.
The First Encounter with the Nauset on Cape Cod happened before the better-known harvest feast with the Wampanoag at Plymouth in 1621, but even that meeting lacked context. The Wampanoag were never invited; 90 warriors arrived and were invited to stay as an act of diplomacy after responding to celebratory musket fire from the colonists.
“The Thanksgiving holiday overlooks a myriad of sins. The backstory to colonization includes enslavement of Native men, the introduction of a devastating plague, the theft of corn and disturbance of graves of the Nauset people, and an alliance that robed the Wampanoag of their sovereignty and land,” Paula Peters, communications and program director at the Native Land Conservancy, said.
The salt marsh and nearby uplands also give a home to vulnerable animals, including diamondback terrapins that nest along the coastal bluffs. The 20.4-acre property next door—bought in June 2026 with help from the Eastham Conservation Foundation and local neighbors—has been named T8nupâhs Uwatuhshât, which means “at the turtle’s nest” in the Wôpanâak language.

items.text:
Texas residents are farming land that isn’t theirs for free in order to raise money to help send kids—who also aren’t theirs—off to college.
As true to the spirit of Thanksgiving as anything you’ll read this week, the 15-year tradition has paid out $3 million in scholarships to hundreds of high schoolers.
“We just treat it like it’s ours—like it’s another one of our farms,” local farmer Derik Grotegut said, referring to the school district’s 640 acres where nearly 1,000 residents work pro bono on one crop of spring corn and one of winter wheat.
Rather than leaving it to family, friends, or a trust, the longtime landowner of those 640 acres left his Texas panhandle farm to the Gruver school district in 1984.
Described by the Washington Post, reporting on the tradition , as a farming community through and through, Gruver’s school district had long leased the farmland to generate income for higher-order school supplies like chemistry beakers and textbooks. It was about 15 years ago that schoolboard members decided to up the ante on their land substantially.
It would require some 1,000 local agriculturalists to make the plan work: an astonishing bet on the sense of commonwealth within the city. The land would be worked, and the crop sold to fund scholarships.
Students from the very beginning of their academic journeys would receive a briefing: excel in school, at volunteering, in extracurricular activities, and earn a bigger share of the crop profits to pay college. The program met with almost instant success, as the Post tells it, with the first decade seeing 48 children become the first in their families to attend university and each annual harvest yielded around $400,000.

“It is unbelievable, the fact that the community will be willing to do this,” Troy Seagler, Gruver High School’s former principal who helped come up with the idea, told the Post.
Farmers indeed volunteer their time, and a Gruver-based feed yard buys their crop at a premium just to swell the scholarship harvest. Meanwhile, 15 years after they started, Gruver grads are bringing their degrees back to town, opening businesses and taking positions according to their new skillsets.
Unsurprisingly, perhaps, many of those who’ve walked off with scholarships often return as farmers, to carry on at the world’s true oldest profession down through the century.

This December, Miami becomes the place to be for art lovers. Art Miami and its sister fair, CONTEXT Art Miami , have just revealed their participating artists and galleries for 2026, and the lineup doesn’t disappoint. Returning to One Herald Plaza, Dec. 1–6, the two fairs will bring together an international mix of galleries, artists, collectors, and contemporary art enthusiasts for the 36th edition of Art Miami and the 14th edition of CONTEXT.
Art Miami 2026 will feature work from galleries hailing from 25 countries, representing major art destinations including London, Paris, Berlin, Seoul, Hong Kong, Dubai, Istanbul, and Bogotá. Visitors can enjoy both modern and contemporary art, from the modern masters and Pop Art icons of the 20th century to contemporary painting , sculpture, photography, design, and new media.
Returning exhibitors include Allouche Gallery , Ascaso Gallery , Boccara Gallery , Ethan Cohen Gallery , and Opera Gallery , alongside more than 20 galleries from Miami and the surrounding South Florida region. Artist Lucy Sparrow will also return following the success of her felt candy store installation at last year’s fair. She will reveal her new installation, The Money Laundry , a hand-felted, interactive laundromat featuring hand-painted cash, passports, and luxury watches.
Meanwhile, CONTEXT Art Miami will once again shine a spotlight on emerging and mid-career artists. Its 14th edition will feature international galleries presenting new and recent works, solo exhibitions, curated projects, and immersive installations. Participating galleries include Bel-Air Fine Art , Hilton Contemporary , Iconic Images Gallery , and Uniquity Art Gallery , among many others.
Another major highlight across both fairs will be the celebration of artist and activist Shepard Fairey , who will receive the 2026 Art Miami Lifetime Visionary Award. Recognized for his influential practice spanning street art, graphic design, and political activism, Fairey will be honored with a curated presentation of his work in Art Miami's VIP Lounge.
Both Art Miami and CONTEXT Art Miami run between Dec. 1–6, at One Herald Plaza in Downtown Miami. Tickets are available online at Art Miami and CONTEXT Art Miami .

items.title: Huge fly-tip grew undetected over several months
items.desc: The council says the 20-tonne pile of rubbish was dumped over garden fences.
items.text:
The waste was dumped over garden fences in South Wigston over several months
Two fly-tippers were able to dump huge amounts of household waste over their garden fences without being detected for several months, with the pile eventually reaching 20 tonnes.
It was spotted on land owned by a business in South Wigston, Leicestershire, earlier in the year.
However, due to the location of the fly-tip, it was not immediately visible to employees of the business, which Oadby and Wigston Borough Council said "allowed the offenders to act over several months".
The two individuals responsible were each issued with a £600 fixed penalty notice following an interview under caution, the authority added, while a third person was cautioned for their role in the offence.
Before the rubbish could be cleared, the council's environmental health officers worked with the business to gather evidence to prove who had been responsible.
The authority has not specified which business was affected by the fly-tipping, or from where the rubbish was sourced.
The waste was reported to Oadby and Wigston Borough Council
The council said it had also recently issued another £600 fine after a resident's waste was found in a lay-by off Gartree Road in Oadby.
They had not fly-tipped the rubbish themselves, the authority added, but had paid a rogue operator in good faith to take it away.
According to the council, residents have a duty of care for their waste until it is disposed of correctly and should ensure it is given to a licensed waste operator.
Councillor Samina Haq, leader of the council, said: "There is simply no excuse for fly-tipping. It damages our environment, costs money to clear up and is unfair on the overwhelming majority of residents and businesses who dispose of their waste responsibly.
"These successful cases send a clear message that we will investigate reports, gather evidence and take action against those responsible.
"Please continue to report fly-tipping whenever you see it and, if you pay someone to remove your waste, always make sure they are properly licensed."

items.title: Floating nature islands installed in parks as Glasgow Games legacy
items.desc: The islands, being planted in five Glasgow parks, are designed to encourage wildlife and help clean the water.
items.text:
Volunteers from local communities have been involved in setting out the plants
Floating islands are being installed on ponds in five of Glasgow's parks as part of the 2026 Commonwealth Games legacy.
The islands, which are being planted by community groups, are designed to encourage wildlife and help clean the water.
The project will create almost 250 square metres of new wildlife habitat which is expected to last about 20 years.
Glasgow 2026 organisers say they are funding the projects as part of their commitment to greener games.
Ellen Hebdon says the plants' roots play an important role in preventing and removing harmful algae from the water
The islands are manufactured by a Moray-based company which has been exporting them around the world.
Biomatrix Water Solutions in Forres has installed islands in Boston, Venice and London.
They have also been floated onto the River Clyde at the Glasgow Science Centre as part of an unrelated project.
The new islands are being installed at Victoria Park, Elder Park, Richmond Park, Queen's Park and Hogganfield Loch.
Ellen Hebdon, the company's operations manager, said the plants' roots played an important role in preventing and removing harmful algae from the water.
"It's not an overnight solution, but over a period of time, you will see benefits in the clarity and the cleanliness of the water," she said.
Floating islands have been installed at the Glasgow Science Centre
The islands are made up of recycled plastic materials, including drinking water pipes, to create buoyancy and are held together using marine-grade stainless steel.
They are then topped with a lightweight clay aggregate, called leca, into which the plants are inserted.
The aquatic plants include a mix of evergreen and flowering native species such as marsh marigolds, water forget-me-nots and ragged robin.
Their roots underneath the islands provide shelter for aquatic wildlife.
The location, in the middle of the water, also provides nesting spaces for birds, which would be largely free from disturbance.
Local schools and "friends of the park" groups are helping with the planting and maintenance.
Games organisers say sustainability is an important delivery factor with all competition venues powered by renewable electricity and electric or hybrid vehicles making up two thirds of the transport fleet.
Glasgow 2026's head of sustainability, Selina Donald, said the city council had been looking at creating floating islands but did not have the funding.

items.text:
Once a year, the owners of a Texas auto-repair shop would refurbish a donated car and then hand the keys to a member of their community in need.
But thanks to their generosity and the generosity of others, they’ve been able to turbocharge their giving, with multiple vehicles going out ever year.
“One was not enough,” says wife Cathy Bailey. “Once we experienced it, you want more,” adds husband Dane.
Indeed, giving away cars is their joy of joys, and something that thanks to their Colleyville community, they can now do multiple times per year.
Autos for Love started years ago when the Baileys, who own Auto Experts of Colleyville , wanted to try and put in a little more elbow grease on behalf of those who have no wheels to grease.
Refurbishing gently used cars donated by community members, their aim was to give away one per year. But seeing the reaction of the recipients quickly pushed them to try and find more cars, and more people in need.
Reported on first by WFAA News , Autos for Love attracted a lot of attention, and soon became turbo-charged with donated vehicles.
This year, the Baileys began looking for who in town needed them the most, and some residents called in to nominate their friend Barbara Farison, a mother whose car was totaled by another motorist running a red light.
Unable to secure a replacement, Farison and her kids have walked everywhere for 3 years when alternative transportation wasn’t available, including to school and to buy groceries. It has exposed them to toil, the elements, and in Farison’s case, to an incident of violent crime she only narrowly avoided.
When her friends got wind of Autos for Love, they called up the Baileys to explain the situation, who then in turn called Farison and invited her to the shop, ostensibly for an “interview.”
Instead, she suddenly found her palms filled with the keys to a 2005 Acura MDX.
“This is the biggest blessing,” Farison said. “I cannot explain to you how much easier this is going to be for my kids and myself. It’s going to make my mommy heart extremely happy.”
Farison was one of 4 people who received cars from the Baileys that day, meaning that this year alone they have given away 8 autos with love.

items.title: 62 Awkward, Funny, Or Straight-Up Weird DMs People Just Couldn’t Keep To Themselves (New Pics)
items.desc: Depending on the moment, a text notification can land differently. When you're swamped, it's a tiny bid for attention you don't have to spare. On a slow day, it's a welcome reminder that someone's thinking of you. But beyond the vanilla "See you at 7" and the low-effort "wyd," your DMs can hold far more than you bargained for, from messages that make you scroll back up to check you read them right
items.text:
Texting might take up a significant portion of our days, but as Caitlin Dewey explains in The Washington Post, it was never supposed to be this big. Communications scholar Colette Snowden found that early phone makers didn't think text messaging would catch on at all. Tapping out messages was a hassle, waiting for a reply was annoying, and the whole thing felt, as Dewey puts it, "so weirdly impersonal."
As it turns out, though, that quiet, reply-whenever-you-feel-like-it vibe was exactly what people loved about it. "The seeming limitations of the SMS system became one of its strengths," Snowden wrote. Because texting was silent, people could use their phones in places where a call just wasn't an option. And psychologically, it had some clear perks, too. You could take your time crafting the perfect reply, and the format forced you to keep things short and sweet.
For writer Sophia Dembling, that makes texts “delightfully positioned in a sweet spot between the telephone and email.” In a piece for Psychology Today, she admits she loves texting, maybe even a little too much, because it lets her control her space and reply when she's ready. Some messages, like memes , don't even need a response; they're just someone's way of saying they saw something and thought of her. “Texts are little dings of connection all day long,” she writes.
But connection isn't the same as clarity. When we text, posture, facial expressions, eye contact, gestures, and even tears are all swapped out for what Dewey calls the "blissful convenience" of a few characters. And according to social psychologist Theresa DiDonato, that's a real problem. Without those nonverbal signals, she explains in Psychology Today, texts are easily misinterpreted .

And we probably misinterpret them more often than we'd like to think. Back in 2005, researchers found that people overestimate both their ability to get their tone across in writing and their ability to read the tone of messages others send them. But when they read the same statement in an email, they got it right just 56% of the time. The reason, the researchers found, is that we can't get out of our own heads. When we type something, we "hear" it exactly the way we meant it, so it's hard to imagine anyone reading it any differently.

items.text:
JoyDrops champions awards-eligible documentary shorts about joy, a counterweight to a category often dominated by tragedy. Good News Network has partnered with JoyDrops to spotlight these films and talk with the filmmakers behind them.
“Believe me, it never gets old,” Freddie Nole told GNN. “I’m serious.”
Nole is talking about the moment he meets a man walking out of prison, often someone with no one else coming to get him. He and his wife, Sue, take the man to a meal, buy him clothes, get him a phone and drive him to wherever he’s headed next. No two pickups are the same, he said, but one thing always is.
“The appreciation that these individuals express to us for just being there,” Nole said, “at a time when they’re most vulnerable.”
That work is at the heart of The Second Life of Freddie Nole , the latest film in GNN’s JoyDrops series.
Directed by Dana Nachman, the film rides along with Nole for a single day as he picks up a man leaving prison in Pennsylvania. Along the way, viewers learn that Nole knows this road personally. His full backstory comes only at the end.
Nachman, whose company, Sweet World Films, focuses on stories about repairing the world, had worked on wrongful conviction cases for years. But reentry was new to her. She and her business partner, Chelsea Matter, had a little money left over from another project and wanted a story that truly fit a short. A one-day road trip was the perfect container.
They reached out to Nole over Zoom. “Literally maybe 30 seconds of talking, I was like, oh God, this guy is special,” Nachman told GNN. “We call him movie gold. Freddie is life gold.”
She later learned that groups across the country do similar work, some just 50 miles from her home in Northern California. She’s glad she didn’t know sooner. “My ignorance got me to him, really,” she said.
Nole went to prison in 1969, when Richard Nixon was president. When he finally walked out, the only person he could count on was his wife, who had stood by him for more than 37 years.
He had sent her his clothing sizes so he wouldn’t stand out. They didn’t fit. “It was just a whole embarrassing situation for me,” he told GNN, “not so much the people, but that I was so detached from this normal society.”
Then he learned he was already in violation of his parole for not reporting in time. He spent four hours of his first night of freedom at the parole office. “My whole first day of being out was simply walking on pins and needles,” he said.

items.text:
In 1967, 33 Massachusetts schoolchildren were given a project: write a letter to a Navy corpsman they had never met who was wounded in Vietnam.
None of them had any idea of the impact their letters had on the veteran, until his son, almost 60 years later, began searching them out.
“I just needed to get back to them and be like, ‘Hey, I know it seems really silly, you’re talking about your pet lizard and you’re saying God bless you, but it made a difference,'” Dave Jacobson tells GNN.
Dave’s father was HM3 Russell Jacobson, who suffered 12 gunshot wounds and shrapnel from a grenade blast. He had been brought home to an understaffed Chelsea Naval Hospital and put in a full-body cast.
Outside, protestors against the Vietnam war heaped abuse on returning servicemen, and for Russell, who Dave described as entering the war as a “pacifist” with the aim of “healing people,” there was a sense of shame, which together with his injuries, began to seep into his very soul.
“He was non-verbal for many weeks and he was refusing food and water, and was down to about 80 pounds. He had lost a dozen of his friends in a couple of hours,” Dave, who wouldn’t be born for another 10 years, explained.
“My mom was a nurse and one of her co-workers was named Kitty. She was always kind of like grasping at straws, like ‘How can we to get this guy back on his feet?'”
“Her sister was a nun at a Catholic school in Gloucester, and she made all the kids write these letters of support.”
It wasn’t as if his father hadn’t been receiving letters: he had, from friends and colleagues, all of whom wrote “kind of what they think they should say.” But it was when Corpsman Russell opened the envelope of 33 letters from St. Ann School and began to leaf through them that, as Kitty said, he began to get back onto his feet.
Slowly, Russell and his wife began to read through the letters, each sealed with a small yearbook-style photo of the author. Ferrari is synonymous with fast cars, but the company is expanding its fleet by dipping its toe into ocean racing. Hypersail is part of Ferrari ’s ambitious move into this form of professional competition, building on its automotive engineering expertise and the demands of high-performance team racing.
The Hypersail is a 100-foot flying ocean monohull, a sailing vessel with a single hull that’s the primary way it stays afloat. Moving a vessel this size above the water requires enormous lift, balance, and speed. Ferrari’s groundbreaking technology is designed to lift the giant vessel off the ocean surface. The team aims to break records and technological barriers. The project has generated 20 patents designed to solve problems involving energy generation, sail handling, aerodynamics, and controlling a 100-foot boat traveling above the water.
The secret behind Hypersail’s ability to rise above the waves lies in three underwater components: its foils, keel, and rudder. Together, these appendages generate lift, maintain balance, and respond to changing sea conditions. The foils act like underwater wings, producing the upward force needed to lift the hull out of the water and reduce drag. The keel incorporates an additional foil with a movable flap that helps manage flight and provides another point of support. Meanwhile, the rudder features a small movable wing that continuously adjusts the boat’s steering.
Hypersail’s flight control system draws on Ferrari’s automotive electronic systems and dynamic control expertise. It automatically analyzes environmental conditions like wind and waves, along with boat speed and heel angle or tilt, to keep the boat stable and balanced no matter the sea’s temperament. This also frees the crew to focus on reading the ocean, making strategic decisions, and finding ways to maximize performance.
Additionally, the racing yacht is designed for energy efficiency. It generates its own electricity using renewable energy sources, including solar panels and wind turbines, for greater self-sufficiency on long ocean voyages.
One of the project’s major long-term ambitions is to set offshore records, potentially including an attempt at the Jules Verne Trophy, the record for the fastest nonstop, unassisted circumnavigation of the globe. The first launch and sea trials are expected in 2027.

The coconut palm is often called the Tree of 1,000 Uses, though ‘school tuition voucher’ is not typically one of those 1,000.
Yet the Faith Christian Academy in Micronesia is, in fact, accepting coconuts in lieu of tuition costs—to help ease the financial burden on families while making use of the ubiquitous fruits that pile up all around.
The Academy’s new tuition plan actually clears 2 hurdles in 1 leap. Students can easily afford tuition while sparing themselves the dangers and toil of fishing to make money. On the other, the coconuts are used by the Academy to rebuild Yap Island’s once-flourishing coconut oil industry.
“Yap is beautiful, but cash is hard to come by,” says Paul Zimmer, founder and CEO of 3 different organizations working on Yap Island, including the Academy. “Almost every family lives off the land and sea. 95% of households grow crops, 88% fish, and 78% grow coconuts, nearly all for their own table.”
“We asked a simple question: what if the thing Yap has in abundance could help pay for the thing families want most for their kids?”
Zimmer would go on to tell GNN that only one-third of all islanders had cash-paying work, most of which was through the government. The notion of a local economy is almost a dream. Everything needed that can’t be grown is imported, and virtually nothing is exported. That wasn’t always the case, however.
According to Zimmer, this island state within the Federated States of Micronesia used to be a large exporter of virgin coconut oil, but slowing exports through the ’90s stopped entirely by the mid-2000s “because prices were low, shipping was poor, and the palms were aging.”
Though the market was gone, the coconuts kept on growing. At the same time, a decade of balancing the books at Faith Christian Academy (FCA) demonstrated that students would often have to work themselves to the bone to afford the tuition costs.
At times, this would involve dangerous nighttime fishing, while at other times it meant double shifts at work for low-wage earners: like the father of Shayalynn, whose family is from the outer island of Ifaluk, but who has attended FCA since 2017.
“I felt relieved and happy about it because my dad didn’t have to work a lot for my tuition,” she said, remembering when she first heard about the coconuts, “The first year that I started in FCA in 2017, he had to work double shifts just to be able to pay for my tuition, the food on the table, and the clothes that I had to wear to school.”

The Smithsonian American Art Museum brings together 225 photographs documenting the United States around its 1976 Bicentennial in Much Here Is Beautiful: Photography Surveys of the U.S. Bicentennial . Featuring work by more than 70 photographers, the exhibition spans the country, from New York City to rural Appalachia. Together, these images capture communities during a period of social and economic change.
The photographs grew out of a federal initiative launched by the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) to mark the nation’s 200th anniversary. Inspired by the Farm Security Administration’s documentary photography during the Great Depression , the program funded 72 regional surveys of American life. The exhibition reunites selections from these projects for the first time, including works rediscovered through curatorial research.
Much Here Is Beautiful also traces the history of federal survey photography. It opens with 19th-century images by Carleton E. Watkins, Timothy O’Sullivan, and William H. Jackson, whose photographs introduced many Americans to the West’s landscapes. Works by Dorothea Lange and Walker Evans show how documentary photography later expanded to record everyday life.
The exhibition spans four regions, from Lee Friedlander’s photographs of industrial towns in the Northeast to Robert Townsend Jones Jr.’s previously unseen images of Beale Street in Memphis. In the Midwest, Joel Meyerowitz photographs St. Louis and its Gateway Arch, while John Margolies documents the roadside attractions that define the American landscape.
In the West, Mark Klett and JoAnn Verburg revisit historic landscapes through their Rephotographic Survey Project, placing contemporary images alongside 19th-century photographs. Reagan Louie’s photographs of San Francisco’s Chinatown offer a more personal perspective on the communities and histories that shape the country.
The exhibition takes its title from Robert Hayden’s 1978 poem “American Journal.” The phrase offers a fitting lens for photographs that look beyond familiar national symbols. Instead, they document the people, places, and everyday experiences that shape American life. Seen together, these images preserve a portrait of the country while inviting viewers to reconsider how its history has been recorded.

items.text:
People have been playing versions of checkers for thousands of years, making it one of the oldest board games still played today . But despite its long history, researchers only recently figured out what happens when the game is played perfectly.
In 2007, a team led by University of Alberta computer scientist Jonathan Schaeffer announced that checkers had been weakly solved ; if both players make the best possible move every time, the game will always end in a draw.
Reaching that conclusion took nearly two decades. Beginning in 1989, Schaeffer and his team used computers to analyze the game, eventually building databases containing around 39 trillion endgame positions. That might sound excessive for a game played on an eight-by-eight board, but checkers is far more complicated than it looks. Researchers estimate around 500 billion possible positions. Rather than calculating every single one, the team worked from both ends. They solved huge numbers of possible endgames while their program searched forward from the standard starting position until the two sets of information connected.
At the center of the project was Chinook, a computer program originally created to compete against the world’s best checkers players. It eventually became strong enough to outperform human opponents, but Schaeffer and his team wanted to go one step further and prove what would happen if both sides played without making a single mistake.
That’s where the term “weakly solved” comes in. The researchers did not solve every possible checkers position. Instead, they proved the outcome from the normal starting position and showed that neither player can force a win when both play perfectly. Of course, that doesn’t mean every game of checkers will end in a draw. Human players make mistakes all the time, leaving plenty of opportunities for someone to triumph.
So while checkers may be mathematically solved, it isn’t exactly ruined. Unless both players can play perfectly, there’s still plenty of game left to play.

items.desc: Changing seasons are affecting wildlife and leading some farmers to grow different crops.
items.text:
The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.
Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost – when the air temperature falls to 0C or below – was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.
In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.
The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.
"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.
"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.
"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."
The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.
Some of the biggest reductions in winter air frosts have been in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where the average number of days has fallen by around 11 compared with 1961 to 1990.
Southern England has seen other significant changes. In Cornwall, the average number of winter air frost days has almost halved, falling from around 18 to just 10.
On the Isle of Wight, the figure has also fallen by almost half, from around 21 to 11 days.
Scotland remains the frostiest UK nation, but has also seen a reduction, from around 45 to 38 winter air frost days.
Summer 2026 was the hottest on record, with five heatwaves
Summer days reaching 25C have become more common across the UK.
Some of the biggest increases have been in southern England, where the average number of summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled, from just over eight to more than 16.
In Essex and Suffolk, they have risen by almost 13 days in both counties.
The Met Office defines a hot day as one where the temperature reaches 30C or above.
Across the UK, the average number of these days has increased fourfold, from 0.3 to 1.2 per summer.
The increase is particularly striking in Greater London, where days reaching 30C have risen from an average of 1.3 to 6.1 per summer.
Summer 2026 was the hottest on record , according to provisional Met Office data.
There were five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C, smashing the previous record of 34 days.

As you scroll through these Black Friday sales disasters, it is worth finding out how this retail chaos started in the first place. Today, the event is a global phenomenon fueled by the internet and e-commerce websites.
It no longer lasts just twenty-four hours, either. Retailers now begin the sales in late October and stretch them across the entire month.
However, Black Friday hasn’t always been about shopping or hunting for the best online bargains.
The very first “Black Friday” had nothing to do with retail stores or Thanksgiving. On September 24, 1869, two Wall Street bankers tried to corner the gold market to make a quick fortune. Their plan backfired, causing a massive market crash and financial panic that earned the day its dark nickname.
The shopping version of the phrase actually came much later. In the 1950s and early 1960s, police officers in Philadelphia used “Black Friday” to describe the chaos that hit the city the day after Thanksgiving. Huge crowds of suburban tourists flooded downtown to start their holiday shopping and attend Saturday’s annual Army-Navy football game. Officers worked long shifts to manage the resulting traffic jams and shoplifting.
Local shopkeepers initially hated the negative name and even tried rebranding the day as “Big Friday.” That failed, so merchants flipped the narrative in the late 1980s. They marked the day stores finally moved from operating at a loss (“in the red”) to turning a yearly profit (“in the black”).
Even though most stores actually made more money on the Saturday before Christmas, the story stuck.
By 2010, Amazon brought Black Friday to the UK — and immediately crashed its own website from the huge volume of buyers.
The tradition is deeply tied to late Thanksgiving, early Christmas shopping and digital convenience. Because it falls right after and before the holidays, millions of people use the weekend to check off their gift lists.
“Holiday shopping continues to be pulled forward, but Thanksgiving weekend remains an important shopping event for consumers,” Allison Zeller, an official at the US-based trade association National Retail Federation, said . “Shoppers are looking for deals, and retailers are delivering great value on gifts while creating special experiences that keep the Thanksgiving weekend shopping tradition going.”

A major success in population-scale control of mosquito-borne viruses comes now from Brazil, where schoolchildren are enjoying a 68% lower risk of such diseases.
The trial tested the largely-proven method of releasing mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia bacteria, which inhibits the insect’s ability to spread viruses like dengue, Zika, and chikungunya.
Trialed over 4 years in Belo Horizonte, the success overlapped with the largest outbreak of dengue fever ever recorded in Brazil, demonstrating the urgent need for greater mosquito control in the tropics.
“The intervention substantially reduced dengue infections during Brazil’s largest recorded outbreak, demonstrating its potential to protect communities even under conditions of intense transmission,” states Derek Cummings, PhD, co-principal investigator of the trial and Bloomberg Distinguished Professor at Johns Hopkins University, one of the institutions that participated.
Called the EVITA dengue trial, the international team set out to test a locally-adapted version of the wMel strain of Wolbachia for use in inhibiting viral transmission from Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
wMel is the most commonly-used strain of Wolbachia, with the ‘Mel’ referring to the fruit fly species from which Wolbachia was first isolated. wMel-infected mosquitoes pass the bacteria to their offspring, thereby inhibiting disease transmission on a generational scale.
EVITA included 58 school-defined geographic clusters in Belo Horizonte, with 29 clusters assigned to receive releases of wMel mosquitoes in addition to standard vector-control measures, and 29 clusters assigned to standard vector control alone, such as insecticidal sprays and mosquito source reduction.
The randomized-controlled trial released Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes from January 2021 through May 2022. It involved 5,757 school children, ages 6 to 11. The results were presented on Saturday at the American Society of Tropical Medicine & Hygiene annual meeting in National Harbor, Maryland.

The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.
The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.
"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."
The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

items.title: 79 Hilarious Science Memes That Make Even The Most Complicated Topics Funny
items.desc: Science isn't that funny. But if you're knowledgeable on it, maybe you can make it funny. Turning everyday knowledge into memes that everyone can enjoy. The full list of hilarious science memes is in the article.
items.text:
Funnily enough, the very origin of the word "meme" actually comes from science itself. Before it became synonymous with relatable, funny images, it was a biological concept coined by evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins .
He combined the Ancient Greek word "mimeme," meaning "something imitated," with the word "gene" to describe how ideas, catchphrases, and cultural behaviors replicate and evolve from brain to brain, much like DNA. Curiously, the term was coined in 1976, long before computers became common and the concept of a meme even existed.
And, as it turns out, using humor has actually been shown to make scientists seem more credible online.
Researchers found that when science communicators used lighthearted, playful humor, like satire, audiences rated them as more likable and more legitimate and trustworthy than those who presented dry facts in a monotone way. Curiously, though, too much harsh sarcasm can backfire and actually reduce trust. Interesting, isn't it?
But research has found more than that about memes and information. Psychological research shows that humor activates the brain's dopamine reward system. This can make engaging with science memes more motivating and enjoyable, while also supporting long-term memory formation.
One survey supporting this idea included 1,637 students across 25 science courses. It found that around 99% appreciated science humor, saying it helped boost their attention and made the subject matter more relatable. So, hey, scrolling through science memes might be a modern way to learn.
Never miss a story that brings joy to the world. Add us on Google
Combining humor and science has also proven to be a great way to get people more interested in learning about science, technology, and the world around them.
In fact, scientists have been using humor to poke fun at their own work for over two centuries. Back in 1802, English caricaturist James Gillray published "Scientific Researches! – New Discoveries in Pneumaticks!", a satirical etching mocking public gas-inhalation demonstrations at London's Royal Institution. Just two years later, geologists were already drawing cartoons poking fun at their rivals' theories.

105 years ago today, Rued Langgaard’s “ Music of the Spheres ” (Sfærernes Musik) premiered at Konzerthaus in Karlsruhe, Germany. Replicating a variety of outer spatial senses through the careful and considered multi-movement work, it includes several methods of orchestral composition well ahead of its time. Several of the movements project the sense of vast space and distance, particularly through the positioning of a small, secondary orchestra off stage. READ more about the work, and listen to it… (1921)
The piece was inspired by a line from a Danish poem translated as, “the stars seem to twinkle kindly at us, yet the writing of the stars is cold and merciless.” Langgard vacates much of the middle tonal range in favor of extreme basso and treble clusters. This lack of depth seems to mimic outer space.
Strings repeatedly stay on single notes, rising and falling in volume as if capturing the orbit of a celestial body. By playing directly on the piano strings, something that had never been done before in orchestra, the musicians plunk out little dampened lights in the darkness of the composition’s vast spaces. It concludes with a sort of end times-like fury, before falling away again to angelic choir and distance.
The premiere was a success, but the following year it received a more lukewarm reception when performed in Berlin. It was not performed again until 1968, where a performance in Stockholm with the Royal Stockholm Philharmonic Orchestra, conducted by Sergiu Comissiona, ignited a renaissance for Langgaard’s music.

items.text:
American conservationists have secured protections for a truly unique-in-the-world ecosystem along the state’s Bering Sea coastline.
Home to the largest concentrations of Pacific walrus found anywhere in North America, the barrier islands off the coast of the tiny northern village of Point Lay provide a critical refuge for these marine megafauna.
Now ensconced within a 47,000-acre protected area (74 square miles) held by the Interior Alaska Land Trust, the islands have been spared from industrial development and other disturbances, as has “one of the largest, undiminished coastal lagoon systems in the world,” which was protected in tandem.
Part of the coalition that for 10 years has worked towards securing protections for the Point Lay barrier islands and the Kasegaluk Lagoon, The Conservation Fund explains that the islands hadn’t historically been a walrus mecca until 2007, when the animals changed their seasonal migration behavior in mass.
Every year, a quarter million Pacific walrus would migrate north through the Bering Strait, with the males remaining out at sea and the females with their calves moving towards the shallow, nutrient-rich waters of the Chukchi Sea between Alaska and Russia.
Historically, these animals relied on Arctic sea ice for resting spots, but by 2007 the ice had become inconsistent. One year, an estimated 200,000 walrus hauled themselves up onto the barrier islands of Point Lay, and they’ve returned every year ever since.
That includes every single female and juvenile Pacific walrus on Earth—all stuffed onto beaches that will now forever be theirs thanks to The Conservation Fund and its partners among the Alaska tribal nations and the Interior Alaska Land Trust.
The new conservation easement was bought by the Fund from an Alaska Native Corporation the Cully Corp. It will be held by the Trust, which will increase monitoring and stewardship to actively minimize disturbance to walrus and other animals as commercial and tourist activity in the Alaskan Arctic continues to expand. Conservation Fund noted that encroachment from humans had already caused undesirable stampede events among the resting animals.

items.title: 101 Maps That Might Leave You A Little Smarter Than You Were Before (New Pics)
items.desc: Maps are usually meant to help us understand the world, but some reveal details we never expected to find. From unusual historical boundaries to surprising statistics and cultural differences, these maps offer a fascinating look at how countries and societies compare. Here are some of the most curious maps that put the world into a whole new perspective.
items.text:
Long before GPS and satellite imagery, people tried to make sense of the world by drawing what they knew. One of the oldest examples is the Babylonian Map of the World , or Imago Mundi. This small clay tablet is from around the sixth century BC.
The tablet shows the world as a circle of land surrounded by water called the Bitter River. Babylon sits in the center, with the Euphrates River running through it. The map also marks nearby lands and far-off places, some linked to Babylonian myths and tales of strange creatures.
Instead of showing an accurate view of the whole planet, the Imago Mundi reflects how Babylonians saw their place in the world. It mixes real places, mythical areas, and religious ideas, showing that early maps were about more than just geography. People used maps to explain the world through their culture.
But maps have always served purposes beyond simply illustrating the world. Some helped people understand their surroundings, while others marked valuable land, key settlements, and borders. A great example is a carved stone slab from the Bronze Age found in Saint-Bélec, Brittany, France, dating to about 2150–1600 BC.
The slab has engraved markings and a raised surface that matches the local landscape. Its makers seem to have mapped an area of about 545 square kilometers. Some markings look like archaeological features from that time, suggesting the carving linked real landmarks to how people organized their land.
This map may have helped show a prehistoric political area and who controlled it. The creators even put the carved slab inside a large burial site, linking it to social status. So, a map could show ownership, influence, and power, not just geography.
Maps also became valuable products, which led to a new problem: competitors could copy someone else's work without permission. To protect their maps , some mapmakers added fake details to catch anyone who copied them. These made-up features included imaginary streets, roads, and even whole towns, called copyright traps or paper towns.
The idea was fairly straightforward and simple. If another company published a map with a place that wasn't real, the original mapmaker could use that fake detail as proof of copying. These made-up spots worked like hidden signatures, helping mapmakers tell their work apart from copies.
A famous example happened in New York in the 1930s , when two workers at the General Drafting Company made up a town called Agloe. They put it at a dirt-road crossing

Wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi encountered the shot of a lifetime in Damaraland, Namibia. In September 2025, he witnessed a desert elephant carrying its stillborn calf. What resulted was an arresting black-and-white image that is beautifully composed but ultimately full of grief. The close-up portrait shows the mother with her deceased calf between her tusk and trunk, as if she is unable to let her baby go. The emotional image, titled The Aftermath , was recognized in the prestigious Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 competition , with Veronesi earning the title of Overall Winner and the Behavior Mammals category winner.
Veronesi was tracking elephants when he noticed an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed. He understood why when he saw the mother and child. “The calf’s body rose up and in this particular frame, it almost looks like the calf is still alive, playing with its mother or trying to cling to her mother’s trunk,” he recalls to My Modern Met. “I feel that the ambiguity of the image, and how it can be read in many ways make it stand out from the other images I took, where the calf is clearly hanging lifeless from the mother’s tusk.”
The photographer initially felt conflicted about capturing the scene. “After taking the first few images, I felt like I was violating the elephant’s intimate moment, her grief, I was almost ashamed and thought that I shouldn’t take these photographs,” he shares. But ultimately, Veronesi found it important to highlight the complexity of these creatures. Elephants have been observed engaging in behaviors around death, including vocalizing, guarding the deceased, and carrying the dead, as pictured. By photographing this painful moment, Veronesi shows us that wildlife and humans aren’t as far apart as we may think.

items.text:
The legendary character of the Silk Road was in full focus recently in Mongolia, where excavations of a nomad’s tomb unearthed objects all the way from Classical Rome.
The tomb undoubtedly belonged to an elite individual from the Xiongnu people, a nomadic group that controlled large stretches of Central Asia, Mongolia, and Manchuria for some 5 centuries.
In addition to a cup made from Roman glass, a gourd-shaped silver and crystal pendant, likely used to adorn a horse’s harness, closely resembles accessories found in tombs on the Korean Peninsula that date to the same period.
The discoveries highlight the Xiongnu’s role in a vast exchange network that linked these progenitors of the conquering Mongols to the Roman Empire, Han China, and the Korean Peninsula.
The Xiongnu’s role in East Asian history cannot be overstated, as much for what these nomadic horse archers did themselves as for what they brought out of their southern neighbors, the Han Chinese. To face down these ferocious warriors, the Chinese stamped their names into the history books with the building of the first Great Wall of China.
A need to secure horses to wage war on the Xiongnu required a stable route to Central Asia, which saw the establishment of Chinese control over the Gansu Corridor. This paved the way for the first iteration of the Silk Road out across the deserts and steppes of the Tarim Basin through to Modern-day Uzbekistan.
The Xiongnu existed as the most powerful confederation of nomadic tribes on the steppe for almost 5 centuries, a span of control unmatched until the rise of Genghis Khan over 1,000 years after their ultimate defeat by the Han.
Located in the Duurlig Nars burial ground, which contains around 300 graves, the newly excavated Tomb 160 is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia to date. The exterior measures nearly 240 feet in length, but the interior chamber is surprisingly small and shallow, extending only about 50 feet deep.
This contrasts with deeper tombs in central Mongolia, suggesting changes in Xiongnu society during the late first and second centuries CE, a period when the empire was declining due to internal conflicts and pressure from the Han military.

items.text:
An Arizona community is celebrating a local grandfather who found a missing toddler in the middle of the cold desert night.
Honored by the sheriff’s office as an outstanding citizen, Jay Stewart said he felt what everyone else who was searching felt, saying “she may not be our child, but she could be.”
The story begins at sundown on November 17th, when, playing with her siblings, 2-year-old Vella Campillo wandered off into the desert surrounding the city of Eloy, wearing nothing but a diaper.
Vella’s parents, Joseph Campillo and Deanna Fritz, contacted police shortly after 5 p.m., saying that she was being looked after by another family member but had gone missing. Any parent can relate: one moment a child is there; the next they’re gone.
Pinal County Sheriff’s Office and local volunteers began to scour the area as night closed in and temperatures began to fall. Among them was father and grandfather Jay Stewart.
“The scariest thing for parents is to lose a child,” Stewart told local news. “I can’t imagine what they were going through.” He added that everyone he met was searching for Vella “for the same reason.”
“We loved her and wanted her back—she may not be our child, but she could be.”
Over the next 7 hours, Stewart, along with his fellow volunteers dozens of members from various law enforcement agencies, searched with flashlights amid 50°F temperatures. Drones and a helicopter were involved in the search, but the child’s miniature heat signature rendered the thermal imaging cameras ineffective.
The breakthrough came just after midnight when Stewart was investigating a line of bushes near a ditch where, unbeknownst to him, little Vella lay curled up. He would later call the Sheriff’s office to signal he’d found the girl, who was taken to the hospital after no small amount of convincing, latched as she was onto Stewart with no desire to let go.
She was reunited with her family shortly after with no injuries or hypothermia.

“To find that little scared child, the way she popped out of that bush, I’ll never forget it as long as I live,” Stewart told KZAS.
In a Facebook video from the Sheriff’s Office, Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple pronounced Stewart “Pinal County’s hero” and awarded him an outstanding citizen certificate. Teeple also made him an honorary member of the Sheriff’s rescue posse.
